'''Abraham Markham Gelbart''' (December 2, 1911 – September 7, 1994) was an American mathematician, the founding dean of the Belfer Graduate School of Science at [[Yeshiva University]] and the namesake of the International Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences at [[Bar-Ilan University]] in [[Ramat Gan]], [[Israel]].<ref name="nyt">{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/12/obituaries/abraham-gelbart-mathematician-82.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|title=Abraham Gelbart, Mathematician, 82|date=September 12, 1994}}.</ref><ref name="rag">{{citation|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199501/people.pdf|first=Allyn|last=Jackson|title=Mathematics People: Abraham Gelbart 1911–1994|journal=[[Notices of the AMS]]|date=January 1995|page=59|volume=42|issue=1}}.</ref>

==Biography==
Gelbart was born to a Polish immigrant family in [[Paterson, New Jersey]].<ref>Staff. [https://library.ias.edu/files/pdfs/hs/cos.pdf#page=174 ''A COMMUNITY OF SCHOLARS: The Institute for Advanced Study Faculty and Members 1930–1980''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111124234612/http://library.ias.edu/files/pdfs/hs/cos.pdf#page=174 |date=2011-11-24 }}, p. 174. [[Institute for Advanced Study]], 1980. Accessed November 20, 2015. "Gelbart, Abe 47–48 M Born 1911 Paterson, NJ."</ref> He dropped out of high school at age 14, but studied mathematics at the [[New York Public Library]], where he came under the mentorship of Yeshiva mathematician [[Jekuthiel Ginsburg]]. Despite not having a high school diploma, he was accepted to [[Dalhousie University]] at age 23, and earned a bachelor's degree there in 1938. He did his graduate studies at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], earning a doctorate in 1940 under the supervision of [[Norbert Wiener]].<ref name="nyt"/><ref name="rag"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Abe Markham Gelbart|id=49284}}</ref>

After taking non-tenure-track positions at [[North Carolina State University|North Carolina State College]], [[Brown University]], and [[NASA]]'s [[Langley Research Center]], Gelbart took a faculty position at [[Syracuse University]] in 1943. He remained there until 1958, when he moved to Yeshiva, taking the position and the editorship of ''[[Scripta Mathematica]]'' both formerly held by his mentor Ginsburg. He retired from Yeshiva in 1979, and took a position as Distinguished Professor at [[Bard College]], where he remained until 1992. He was also a trustee of Bar-Ilan university.<ref name="rag"/> His doctoral students include [[Robert Finn (mathematician)|Robert Finn]]. Gelbart died from complications following [[cardiac surgery|cardiovascular surgery]].<ref name="mac">{{MacTutor|id=Gelbart|title=Abraham Markham Gelbart}}</ref>

==Mathematics==
With [[Lipman Bers]], Gelbart founded the theory of [[pseudoanalytic function]]s in [[fluid dynamics]].<ref name="nyt"/><ref name="rag"/><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199501/bers.pdf|first=William|last=Abikoff|title=Remembering Lipman Bers: Lipman Bers|journal=[[Notices of the AMS]]|date=January 1995|pages=8–18|volume=42|issue=1}}.</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Gelbart was given an honorary doctorate by Dalhousie University in 1972, and by Bar-Ilan University in 1985. In 1981, Bard College gave him the Bard Medal.<ref name="rag"/>

==Personal life==
Gelbart is the father of [[Stephen Gelbart]], also a noted mathematician.<ref name="mac"/> He is also the uncle of mathematician [[Charles Fefferman]].<ref name="m560">{{cite journal | last=Fefferman | first=Charles L. | title=Twentieth Century Geometry | website=Bard Digital Commons | date=1984-04-14 | url=https://digitalcommons.bard.edu/dsls_1983_1984/3/ }}</ref>
